pages.c10-p02: Describe how gaming applications, simulations and mobile phone applications can be used to support education and training, social interactions and work practices
pages.c10-p03: Describe how virtual reality is used to create realistic simulations for training
pages.c10-p04: Evaluate the impact of online banking on customers and on banks
pages.c10-p05: Evaluate the impact of online training on employees and employers
pages.c10-p06: Evaluate the impact of e-commerce on customers and on businesses

q.q: What is a simulation?
o: A computer model that copies how a real object or system behaves
A video recording of a real event that can be replayed
A game in which players compete on an online leaderboard
A phone app that uses GPS to show the user's position
q.why: A simulation uses a computer model, data plus mathematical rules, to copy how a real system behaves.

q.q: What does a computer model consist of?
o: Large amounts of data plus mathematical rules
A headset, headphones and data gloves
Points, badges and a leaderboard
A touch screen, GPS and a camera
q.why: A computer model is large amounts of data plus mathematical rules; a headset and gloves are VR hardware.

q.q: Which game feature tells players straight away how well they have done?
o: An avatar
Immediate feedback
Levels
Real-time chat
q.why: Immediate feedback shows the result of each action at once, so the player can decide what to try next.

q.q: What does a leaderboard do in a game?
o: Lets players talk to each other in real time
Ranks players' scores, which motivates them to improve
Stops players moving on until a level is finished
Lets players take on the role of a character
q.why: A leaderboard ranks players and motivates them to improve.

q.q: Which statement describes how levels work in a game?
o: Players can choose any level to play in any order
Each level is easier than the one before it
Levels are only used in games with no rules
Each level is harder, and one must be finished before moving on
q.why: Levels get harder and must be completed in order.

q.q: Which feature of games lets players take on a role as a character?
o: Leaderboards
Push notifications
Levels
Avatars
q.why: Rich multimedia and avatars let players take on roles.

q.q: Which is a feature of mobile phone apps rather than of simulations?
o: A mathematical model of a bridge
Crash-testing virtual cars
Repeating a flight emergency
Push notifications
q.why: Push notifications are a typical mobile app feature; the others are uses of simulations.

q.q: Why are push notifications useful in a mobile app?
o: Users can find information on a small screen
The app keeps working without a signal
Alerts and reminders arrive instantly
The app can show the user's location
q.why: Push notifications deliver alerts and reminders instantly.

q.q: A walking app records a route even with no signal on a mountain and uploads it later. Which app feature is this?
o: Push notifications
Personalisation
Search and filter
Offline use with cloud sync
q.why: Offline use with cloud sync lets work continue without signal and update later.

q.q: A user changes an app's layout and chooses which news topics appear first. Which feature is this?
o: Search and filter
Offline use
Push notifications
Personalisation
q.why: Personalisation lets users change settings, layout and content to suit them.

q.q: Why do many apps include search and filter tools?
o: To send alerts and reminders to the user
To let the app work without a signal
To find information quickly on a small screen
To track the user's position using GPS
q.why: Search and filter help find information quickly on a small screen.

q.q: A takeaway app shows the nearest restaurants to the user. Which built-in sensor does it rely on?
o: The camera
The microphone
GPS
The touch screen
q.why: GPS gives location-aware services.

q.q: Why do car makers crash-test virtual cars?
o: Virtual cars are stronger than real cars, so they pass more often
Real crash tests are not allowed by law in the UK
Simulations do not need any data or mathematical rules
Conditions can be changed and tests repeated without real-world risk or cost
q.why: Simulations let users change conditions, run 'what if?' tests and repeat scenarios without real-world risk or cost.

q.q: Where is a mobile app usually downloaded from?
o: A data centre
A leaderboard
A file server
An app store
q.why: Mobile apps are usually downloaded from an app store.

q.q: Which description of a game feature would earn two marks?
o: A leaderboard ranks players' scores, which motivates them to improve
A leaderboard is a feature found in many popular games
Leaderboards are good and players really like them
A leaderboard, levels and avatars are all game features
q.why: 'Describe a feature' needs the feature and what it does for the user.

q.q: Engineers want to see how a new bridge copes with a storm before it is built. What should they use?
o: A mobile app
A leaderboard
A simulation
A gaming application
q.why: Engineers use simulations to test how a bridge or building copes with storms, floods or earthquakes before it is built.

q.q: Which feature of games supports real-time communication between players?
o: Immediate feedback after each move
Levels that get harder in turn
Headsets with voice and text chat
Points awarded for good play
q.why: Real-time communication uses headsets, voice and text chat, and online groups or clans.

q.q: Adding points, badges and leaderboards to a non-game task to motivate people is called...
o: simulation
gamification
virtual reality
streaming
q.why: Gamification applies game features to everyday tasks, such as team leaderboards at work.

q.q: Which is an example of a mobile app supporting work practices?
o: A pupil plays a racing game against friends after school
A family video-calls a relative who lives in Australia
A manager sends an instant announcement to all staff in a group
A teenager streams music on the bus to school
q.why: Group messaging and announcements support communication at work. The others are social or leisure uses.

q.q: Why are games built in levels useful for training?
o: Learners can skip straight to the hardest part at once
Skills are built step by step as each level adds a challenge
Learners are given no feedback, so they think for themselves
Each level repeats the same task with no new challenge
q.why: You cannot skip a level, so skills are built in order, and each level brings a new challenge.

q.q: Why do mistakes in a training game help learners?
o: They have no real consequences, so learners can take risks and reflect
They are hidden from the learner so that confidence stays high
They cost the learner points, which ends the game immediately
They are sent to the employer, who decides on a punishment
q.why: Mistakes in a game have no real consequences, so learners can take risks and reflect on their choices.

q.q: Pupils use a virtual chemistry lab to mix chemicals that would be dangerous in school. Which area does this support?
o: Social interaction
Education and training
Work practices
E-commerce
q.why: Simulations let pupils experiment safely, supporting education and training.

q.q: Friends in different countries play an online game together and chat in real time. Which area does this support?
o: Social interaction
Work practices
Education and training
Online banking
q.why: Online multiplayer lets friends compete or co-operate worldwide while chatting in real time.

q.q: A plumbing firm's staff log each finished job on an app while on site. Which area does this support?
o: Social interaction
Education and training
Gaming
Work practices
q.why: Logging jobs on site with an app is an example of mobile apps supporting work practices.

q.q: How can simulations support work practices?
o: Trainees practise dangerous or rare tasks and designers test products virtually
Staff send instant announcements and share calendars on their phones
Friends meet as avatars in a shared virtual world after work
Pupils revise using quizzes that are saved in the cloud
q.why: In work, simulations let trainees practise dangerous or rare tasks and let designers test products before building them.

q.q: How can mobile apps support education?
o: Trainee pilots practise engine failures in a full-size cockpit simulator
Staff are given badges and team leaderboards to raise motivation
Teachers share video and e-books, and work is saved in the cloud for home and school
Car makers crash-test virtual cars before they build real ones
q.why: Mobile apps let teachers share video, audio and e-books, revision apps quiz pupils, and work is saved in the cloud.

q.q: Which is a risk of gaming and apps that should be mentioned when evaluating them?
o: Immediate feedback
Step-by-step levels
Cloud saves
Contact with strangers
q.why: Risks include addiction and lost sleep, contact with strangers, in-game spending, cyberbullying and distraction.

q.q: Which measure reduces the risk of in-game spending by children?
o: Turning on immediate feedback
Adding more levels to the game
Spending limits and parental controls
Joining an online clan
q.why: Privacy settings, parental controls and spending limits reduce the risks.

q.q: A company adds team leaderboards and badges to its sales targets. What is the main aim?
o: To raise staff motivation
To train staff for dangerous tasks
To test products before building them
To let staff work offline
q.why: Gamification of work tasks can raise staff motivation.

q.q: Examiners often find that answers on this topic forget one of the three areas. Which one?
o: Education and training
Work practices
Social interactions
Gaming
q.why: Answers often forget work practices, so learn an example for every cell of the grid.

q.q: Which answer best links a feature to a benefit for training?
o: Immediate feedback is a feature of games that is used for training trainees
Training games are fun and trainees enjoy using them during work hours
Games have levels, leaderboards and avatars, which are all useful features
Immediate feedback lets the trainee see straight away what went wrong, so they improve faster
q.why: Always link the feature to the benefit: what it does and why that helps the learner.

q.q: Shared virtual worlds where people meet as avatars mainly support which area?
o: Work practices
Online banking
Social interaction
E-commerce
q.why: Shared virtual worlds let people meet as avatars, supporting social interaction.

q.q: A school sends parents a message about a sports day through its app. Which area does this show?
o: Social interaction
Education and training
Work practices
Gaming
q.why: Schools messaging parents about events is listed under work practices for mobile apps.

q.q: Why does each new level of a game keep a learner interested?
o: Each level brings a new challenge
Each level gives the same reward
Each level can be skipped at once
Each level hides the learner's score
q.why: Each level brings a new challenge, keeping the learner interested.

q.q: What does virtual reality create?
o: A flat 2D video of a real place shown on a phone screen
A leaderboard that ranks the scores of different players
A computer-generated 3D world the user feels they are inside
A list of alerts and reminders sent to a mobile device
q.why: VR uses a simulation to create a computer-generated 3D world that the user feels they are inside.

q.q: How does a VR headset make the view change as the user looks around?
o: It shows one image to both eyes and tracks hand movement
It shows a separate image to each eye and tracks head movement
It vibrates when the user turns their head to one side
It plays sound through headphones to guide the user
q.why: A VR headset shows a separate image to each eye and tracks head movement.

q.q: What is immersion in virtual reality?
o: Stimulating several senses so the experience feels real
Running a simulation without any headset at all
Recording every action so it can be replayed later
Ranking users' scores on an online leaderboard
q.why: Stimulating several senses makes VR feel real; this is called immersion.

q.q: Which VR device tracks hand movements and can give touch feedback through vibration?
o: Data gloves
A VR headset
Headphones
A touch screen
q.why: Data gloves or handheld controllers track hand movements and can give touch feedback.

q.q: Which statement about simulation and VR is correct?
o: VR and simulation mean exactly the same
VR is one way of experiencing a simulation
A simulation always needs a VR headset
VR involves only the sense of sight
q.why: A simulation is the computer model; VR is one immersive way of experiencing it. A flight simulator can use real controls without a headset.

q.q: How is a 3D virtual patient for surgical training usually created?
o: From photographs found on social media
From data collected by body scanners
By drawing it in a paint program
From the patient's GP referral letter
q.why: Scan data is turned into an accurate 3D model of the patient.

q.q: What is the main reason airlines train pilots for engine failures in simulators?
o: Emergencies can be practised with no risk to life and no fuel cost
Simulators let pilots skip supervised practice in real aircraft
Simulators remove the need for any instructors to be present
Real aircraft are not allowed to fly in bad weather conditions
q.why: Safety and cost are the key benefits of simulator training.

q.q: A trainee firefighter repeats the same VR scenario until confident. Which benefit of VR training is this?
o: Rare events on demand
Cost
Repetition
Immersion
q.why: Scenarios can be repeated until the trainee is confident.

q.q: An emergency that might happen once in a pilot's career can be practised every week in a simulator. Which benefit is this?
o: Rare events on demand
Repetition
Feedback
Cost
q.why: Rare emergencies can be practised whenever needed.

q.q: After a VR training session, the instructor replays the trainee's actions to review them. Which benefit is this?
o: Feedback
Safety
Cost
Immersion
q.why: Every action is recorded so the trainee and instructor can replay and review it.

q.q: Which is a cost benefit of VR training for an airline?
o: VR equipment is cheap to buy and the software is free
No fuel is used and no aircraft is taken out of paid service
Trainees no longer need any real-world practice
Instructors are not needed during VR sessions
q.why: VR training uses no fuel and no aircraft is taken out of paid service; VR equipment itself can be expensive.

q.q: Which is a limitation of VR training?
o: Scenarios cannot be repeated more than once
Every action is recorded for later review
Dangerous tasks can be practised safely
Some users experience motion sickness or eye strain
q.why: Limitations include cost, not copying real pressure or fear, motion sickness or eye strain, and still needing real practice.

q.q: Why do trainees still need supervised real-world practice after VR training?
o: VR cannot show three-dimensional images to the trainee
VR does not let scenarios be repeated more than once
VR cannot copy every real feeling, such as real pressure or fear
VR does not record the trainee's actions for feedback
q.why: VR cannot copy every real feeling, so supervised real-world practice is still needed.

q.q: A good answer to a VR training question should include which three things?
o: The price of the headset, the brand of the software, and the trainee's age
The history of VR, the inventor of the headset, and the year it was made
The number of levels, the leaderboard ranking, and the badges awarded
The hardware, what the trainee practises, and why it is better than real practice
q.why: Name the hardware, explain what the trainee practises, and give a reason it is better, such as safety, cost, repetition or feedback.

q.q: Which senses does VR stimulate?
o: Sight only
Sight, hearing and sometimes touch
Hearing and smell only
Touch and taste only
q.why: VR stimulates sight, hearing and sometimes touch through headsets, headphones and gloves or controllers.

q.q: A flight simulator uses real cockpit controls and large screens but no headset. Which statement is correct?
o: It cannot be a simulation, because simulations always use VR
It is a simulation, but not one experienced through a VR headset
It is virtual reality, because it uses a computer model
It is not useful for training, because it lacks immersion
q.why: A simulation is the model; VR is one way to experience it. A flight simulator can work without a headset.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of online banking for the customer?
o: Access is available 24/7
Transfers can be made instantly
Spending alerts help budgeting
Phishing attacks may steal login details
q.why: Phishing is a risk; the others are advantages.

q.q: Which is a benefit of online banking for the BANK?
o: Fewer branches and staff are needed, cutting costs
The customer avoids travelling and queuing
The customer can manage money from abroad
The customer receives instant spending alerts
q.why: Lower building and wage costs benefit the bank. The other options benefit the customer.

q.q: Why do banks use two-factor authentication for online banking?
o: To check it really is the customer, using two different methods
To make payments between UK accounts arrive almost instantly
To let customers print their statements at home
To replace the need to encrypt data sent to the bank
q.why: 2FA uses a second check, such as a code or fingerprint, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

q.q: What does Faster Payments allow?
o: Customers to set up a new account in one day
Money to move between UK accounts almost instantly
Banks to close branches more quickly
Customers to log in without a password
q.why: Faster Payments moves money between UK accounts almost instantly.

q.q: Why are some older or less confident people excluded by online banking?
o: It is only available during normal branch hours
It needs a device, internet access and digital skills
It charges a fee for each transaction made online
It does not allow bills to be paid from an account
q.why: Online banking needs a device, internet access and digital skills, which some people do not have.

q.q: Which is a negative impact of online banking on banks?
o: Their customers can only bank when branches are open
They must build and keep updating complex security systems
They must post paper statements to every customer
They can only serve customers who live near a branch
q.why: Banks must invest heavily in security systems and specialist staff.

q.q: How do e-statements benefit a bank?
o: They stop all phishing attacks
They remove the need for 2FA
They mean fewer customers
They save paper and postage
q.why: E-statements save the bank paper and postage.

q.q: Why does online banking let a bank's customer base grow?
o: Customers must visit a branch to register
Customers do not need to live near a branch
Banks can charge more for online accounts
Only new customers can use online banking
q.why: Because customers do not need to live near a branch, the bank can attract customers from a wider area.

q.q: Why is the large store of customer data held by an online bank a risk to the bank?
o: It slows down every transaction made by customers
It must be printed and posted to customers each month
It stops the bank from using two-factor authentication
It is a target, and a breach damages trust and brings fines
q.why: Large stores of personal data are a target; a breach damages trust and brings fines.

q.q: What is the wider impact of online banking on rural communities?
o: Branch closures remove local jobs and face-to-face services
More branches open in villages to support online users
Rural customers get faster broadband from the banks
Rural customers can no longer use online banking
q.why: Branch closures hit rural communities and older people hardest, removing local jobs and face-to-face services.

q.q: A customer is abroad and her phone has no signal when she needs to pay a bill online. Which disadvantage of online banking does this show?
o: Banks charge more for transactions made from abroad
Faster Payments do not work between UK accounts
Encryption stops payments being made from abroad
No signal or an outage means no access to money when needed
q.why: A website outage or no signal means no access to money when it is needed.

q.q: Which security feature of online banking protects a customer who forgets to log out?
o: Faster Payments
E-statements
Automatic log-out
Spending alerts
q.why: Encryption, 2FA, automatic log-out and fraud alerts protect accounts.

q.q: What does 'evaluate' require in an exam answer on online banking?
o: List as many advantages as possible
Describe only the disadvantages
Explain how to open an online account
Weigh both sides and reach a judgement
q.why: 'Evaluate' means weigh both sides and reach a judgement.

q.q: A pupil writes 'Online banking is faster.' How could it be improved?
o: Say that online banking is also easier and better than going to a branch
Add that online banking uses the internet and a computer or phone
Nothing, because 'faster' on its own is a full answer to an evaluate question
Say what is faster and why it matters, e.g. instant transfers mean bills are paid on time
q.why: 'It's faster' alone earns nothing; say what is faster and why it matters to that person.

q.q: Which is a negative impact of online banking on customer support?
o: Help pages and chat are only available during normal office hours each weekday
Customers must travel to a branch every time they need help with a payment
Customers have to pay a fee each time they use the bank's online chat
There is no face-to-face help, and some customers do not trust a system with no person involved
q.why: Chat and help pages are available any time, but there is no face-to-face help, and some customers do not trust it.

q.q: Which pair contains one customer advantage and one bank advantage of online banking?
o: Spending alerts; instant transfers
E-statements; fewer staff needed
Phishing risk; costly security
24/7 access; fewer branches needed
q.why: 24/7 access helps customers and fewer branches cuts the bank's costs. The other pairs are both on one side or are disadvantages.

q.q: Which is an example of two-factor authentication when logging in to a banking app?
o: A PIN plus a fingerprint
A username plus a password
A password typed in twice
A username plus a PIN
q.why: 2FA uses two different types of check, such as a PIN plus a code or fingerprint. A username with a password or PIN is a single check.

q.q: What is online training?
o: Training given face to face by an instructor at a training venue
A game played online by friends who chat in real time
Buying and selling training courses using an online shop
Learning delivered over the internet, such as videos, modules and quizzes
q.why: Online training is learning delivered over the internet, completed on a computer, tablet or phone.

q.q: Which feature lets managers see which modules each employee has completed?
o: Gamification
Cloud gaming
Automatic tracking
Faster Payments
q.why: Automatic tracking records modules completed and test scores without extra paperwork.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of online training for employees?
o: Help may be limited to FAQs or email
They can learn at their own pace
They do not need to travel
The content uses engaging multimedia
q.why: Without face-to-face support, learners may wait for replies and feel isolated.

q.q: Why is setting deadlines difficult with online training?
o: Computers cannot store or display dates
Staff work at different paces, even on different modules
Employers are not allowed to set deadlines
Online modules never have an end
q.why: Self-paced learning makes common deadlines hard to set.

q.q: A retail chain wants staff in all 20 branches to complete the same new training this week. Which advantage of online training helps most?
o: Content includes video and animation
Training works on mobile devices
Staff in different branches can train at once
Learners can revisit hard parts
q.why: Staff in different branches can train at the same time, so everyone gets the same training quickly.

q.q: Why does online training save both the employee and employer money and time?
o: Staff no longer need any practical skills
There is no travel to a training venue
Employers no longer need to monitor progress
There are no costs for broadband or devices
q.why: No travel saves staff time and travel costs, benefiting both sides.

q.q: Which disadvantage of online training mainly affects the employee?
o: Deadlines are hard to set for the whole team
It needs self-motivation, because it is easy to put off
There is less sense of control over engagement
Completion can be tracked but not real effort
q.why: Needing self-motivation affects the employee; deadlines and control are employer issues.

q.q: Why does an employer have 'less sense of control' with online training?
o: It cannot see which modules each member of staff has finished
It has no way of giving staff any tests or quizzes at all
It must ask an outside company to approve every module
It can track completion but not how well staff really engaged
q.why: Managers can track completion but not how well staff really engaged with the material.

q.q: Which disadvantage of online training affects both employees and employers?
o: Help is limited to FAQs and emails
It needs a lot of self-motivation
Deadlines are hard to set
It depends on technology such as a reliable connection
q.why: Depending on technology affects both: a poor connection or out-of-date browser stops learning.

q.q: Why does online training not suit everyone?
o: Some people learn better with a trainer or hands-on practice
Online training never includes any video or sound
Online training must be completed in one sitting
Online training can only be taken in a classroom
q.why: It does not suit every learning style; some learn better with a trainer or hands-on practice.

q.q: How can online training let staff practise risky tasks realistically?
o: Through automatic tracking of module scores
Through VR simulations, such as flight simulators
Through FAQs and email support from trainers
Through deadlines set for the whole team
q.why: VR simulations give realistic practice of risky tasks.

q.q: A question asks for advantages of online training to the EMPLOYER. How should 'learn at your own pace' be used?
o: Link it to the employer, e.g. less time away from the shop floor
Write it as it is, because it is always an employer advantage
Leave it out, because it can never be linked to the employer
Replace it with 'the employee enjoys it more than a course'
q.why: Employee-focused points only earn credit for the employer if linked to the employer.

q.q: What has made online training far more practical in recent years?
o: Paper workbooks
More training venues
Faster broadband
Longer deadlines
q.why: Faster broadband has made online training far more practical.

q.q: Why are practical skills hard to learn fully through online training?
o: Real-world practice is still needed
Online videos cannot show practical tasks
Practical skills cannot be tracked at all
Employers are not allowed to test them
q.why: Practical skills need real-world practice, which online training cannot fully replace.

q.q: Which benefit of online training helps an employee with young children most?
o: Automatic tracking of the modules completed
Training staff in many branches at once
Learning at a convenient time that fits around family
Deadlines that are set for the whole team
q.why: Learning at a convenient time and own pace fits around work and family.

q.q: How does multimedia in online training help employees?
o: It lets managers track how many modules were done
It makes content engaging and easier to understand
It removes the need for any internet connection
It sets a single deadline for all staff to meet
q.why: Video, animation and sound make content engaging and easier to understand.

q.q: What is e-commerce?
o: Sending marketing emails to a business's customers
Managing a bank account using a website or an app
Buying and selling goods and services over the internet
Delivering training to staff over the internet
q.why: E-commerce is electronic commerce: buying and selling online.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of e-commerce for the customer?
o: Shopping is possible 24 hours a day
Price-comparison sites help decisions
There is a wider choice of products
Goods cannot be seen or tried before buying
q.why: Goods may not match the photos and must be posted back. The others are advantages.

q.q: Why can online businesses often charge lower prices?
o: They never have to pay any delivery or warehouse costs
They are not required to keep their websites secure
They do not need expensive high-street shops or checkout staff
They are only allowed to sell digital goods online
q.why: Lower premises and staff costs can be passed on as lower prices.

q.q: Why is e-commerce especially helpful for people with disabilities or rural customers?
o: They can shop 24/7 without travelling
They get free delivery on every order
They can try goods on before buying
They do not need an internet connection
q.why: Shopping 24/7 without travelling helps people with disabilities, parents of young children and rural customers.

q.q: How do secure payment services such as PayPal protect online shoppers?
o: Goods can be returned without any postage
Fake websites are removed from the internet
Card details are not shared with the seller
Delivery is guaranteed by a set date
q.why: Secure payment services mean card details are not shared with the seller.

q.q: Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, how long do online shoppers usually have to cancel most goods?
o: 7 days from ordering them
28 days from paying for them
30 days from receiving them
14 days from receiving them
q.why: Online shoppers can usually cancel most goods within 14 days of receiving them, though they may have to pay return postage.

q.q: A customer orders a £20 item with an £8 delivery charge. Which disadvantage of e-commerce does this show?
o: Goods cannot be seen or tried before they are bought
Fake websites may steal the customer's card details
Delivery charges can make goods dearer than the advertised price
Parcels may be late or missed at busy times
q.why: Delivery charges can make goods cost more than the advertised price: here £28 rather than £20.

q.q: Which is an advantage of e-commerce for businesses?
o: Customers worldwide and open 24/7, so more potential sales
No need to build or maintain a secure website
No competition from sellers in other countries
Returns and refunds cost the business nothing
q.why: Global reach and opening 24/7 give more potential sales.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of e-commerce for businesses?
o: Customers can leave reviews that attract buyers
Strong competition from global sellers
Sales data shows which products sell well
No high-street shop is needed
q.why: Strong global competition is a disadvantage; the others are advantages.

q.q: How do customer reviews affect an online business?
o: Reviews have no effect on whether customers buy
Only bad reviews are shown to other customers
Good reviews attract buyers, but bad reviews spread quickly
Reviews stop customers returning goods
q.why: Reviews attract new buyers, but bad reviews spread quickly.

q.q: What is a wider impact of e-commerce on society?
o: All high-street shops close and no new jobs are created anywhere
High streets grow because more people collect parcels there
Some high-street shops close, though warehouse and delivery jobs are created
Town centres are not affected because shops stay the same
q.why: Some high-street shops close, affecting town centres and local jobs, though warehouse, delivery and web jobs are created.

q.q: A question asks only for disadvantages of e-commerce for CUSTOMERS. Which point would earn nothing?
o: Businesses face strong competition from global sellers
Goods may not match the photos and must be posted back
Parcels may be late or missed at Christmas
Fake websites can steal card details
q.why: Points about the business earn nothing when the question is about customers.

q.q: Which customer advantage of e-commerce lets a gamer get a popular new game on release day?
o: Using price-comparison sites
Paying with a secure service
Pre-ordering items before release
Reading customer reviews
q.why: Customers can pre-order popular items, such as games, before release.

q.q: Which is a security risk of e-commerce for customers?
o: Card details are hidden from the seller
Fake websites can steal card details
Payments use a secure service
Prices can be compared easily
q.why: Fake websites and data breaches at retailers are risks; the others protect customers or help them.

q.q: Why must an online business spend money on warehousing and delivery?
o: The law requires every online business to own its own delivery vans
Goods must be stored and sent to customers rather than collected in a shop
Warehouses are needed to host the business's website servers
Customers must visit the warehouse to try the goods before buying
q.why: Online businesses must pay for warehousing and delivery as well as a secure website and payment system.

q.q: How does sales data help an online business?
o: It shows which products sell well
It stops customers leaving bad reviews
It removes the need for a secure website
It reduces delivery times for customers
q.why: Sales data shows what sells, helping the business decide what to stock.

q.q: Which statement correctly compares one customer impact and one business impact of e-commerce?
o: Customers pay no delivery charges; businesses pay no website costs
Customers get wider choice; businesses must pay for returns and refunds
Customers can try goods first; businesses avoid all competition
Customers wait less for goods; businesses need more high-street shops
q.why: Wider choice is a customer advantage and returns costs are a business disadvantage. The other options contain statements that are untrue.
